_instructions: One file for every article detail page (article.html?id=<slug>). Mirror of data/case-studies.json conventions: top-level article array, stable string ids (slugs), plain-paragraph body text (blank line separates paragraphs — the renderer escapes and wraps them, no raw HTML). To publish: copy a record, set a unique id, fill title/excerpt/date, describe mainImage {src, alt, caption}, write 3–5 sections, save. No code changes needed. Story images: 1200 x 800 px (3:2), WebP/JPG/AVIF under 250 KB, key content in the central 80%; every story image needs both real alt text AND a caption — they are different things. Sections take at most one image ({src, alt, caption}), rendered under the heading before the body; omit it and the section renders with no gap. 'related' takes article ids (internal cards) or full https URLs (new-tab links); unknown ids are skipped.

articles.title: Agro-Processing in Malawi: Untapped Potential in a Growing Sector
articles.excerpt: What the data behind agro-processing investment means for policymakers and investors in Malawi.

mainImage.alt: Packaged, processed agricultural goods arranged for display
mainImage.caption: Agro-processed goods on display in Malawi. Most of what the country harvests still leaves the farm gate with little value added.

sections.heading: Why agro-processing matters now
sections.body:
Agriculture remains the backbone of Malawi's economy, yet most of what the country grows leaves the farm gate with little value added. Agro-processing — turning raw crops into packaged, graded and shelf-ready goods — is where farm incomes, jobs and export earnings are won or lost.

This piece looks at the numbers behind the sector and what they mean for policymakers and investors weighing where to put their next kwacha.

sections.heading: What the data shows
sections.body:
Malawi's agro-processing base is narrow relative to the size of its harvest. A small number of product lines dominate formal processing, while large volumes of perishable produce move through informal channels with no cold chain, grading or packaging.

Benchmarking against regional peers underlines the gap: countries that invested early in processing infrastructure capture far more value per tonne harvested, and their processors anchor rural employment well beyond the farm.

image.alt: A basket of packaged grocery items on a store shelf
image.caption: A standard basket of grocery items in a Malawian store. Formal retail sets the volume and consistency bar that local processors must meet.

sections.heading: The constraints holding it back
sections.body:
Reliable power, access to finance for processing equipment, and consistent quality standards come up in every conversation with operators. Post-harvest losses remain high for perishables, and small processors struggle to meet the volume and consistency requirements of formal retail and export buyers.

None of these constraints is new — but taken together they explain why investment has flowed more slowly than the opportunity justifies.

sections.heading: What would unlock investment
sections.body:
The opportunity sits at the intersection of three moves: targeted infrastructure for aggregation and cold storage, finance products sized for small and mid-size processors, and standards support that helps local brands reach supermarket shelves.

For policymakers, the prize is rural jobs and import substitution. For investors, it is an early position in a sector whose fundamentals — land, labour and unmet demand — already point in the right direction.

articles.pullQuote: Malawi doesn't have a harvest problem. It has a value-addition problem — and that is precisely where the opportunity lies.
